description: Team MANTA is building real-time health monitoring software for deep-space astronauts. We bring strong expertise in full-stack architecture, AI, and software development. We are looking for teammates skilled in UI/UX design, data visualization, and biomedical engineering to turn telemetry into actionable space insights. Join us .
summary:
Astra Vigil 2.0 is early-warning software for astronaut health on long space trips. On Mars, a message to
Earth can take up to 22 minutes one way, so a crew cannot always wait for Mission Control. Our software
runs on one small computer inside the spacecraft and needs no internet. Each day it reads six body
signals: heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV), blood oxygen, sleep, core temperature and exercise. It
compares each astronaut with their own last 30 normal days, not with a crowd average. If a signal moves
far from that person's normal, the console shows a clear alert and explains why, using saved NASA
research records. It never diagnoses and never predicts an emergency. It uses simple math rules, not AI,
so every alert can be checked. Privacy comes first: the astronaut sees the raw numbers, and others see
only a short status word. All our tests use simulated data. Astra Vigil 2.0 is a decision-support idea, not a
medical device

WHAT IT IS

Astra Vigil 2.0 is early-warning software for astronaut health on long space trips. It runs on one small computer inside the spacecraft (a Raspberry Pi 5 or a Jetson Orin Nano) and works with no internet. It does not diagnose and it does not predict emergencies. It says only one thing: "this person is drifting away from their own normal."

 

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Cuando la Tierra guarda silencio: en la Academia de Ciencias de Rusia se desarrolla protección contra el estrés en el espacio" ]

THE PROBLEM

On the International Space Station, crew health is watched mostly by ground teams in Mission Control. That works well near Earth. On Mars, NASA says a message can take up to 22 minutes one way, so a question and answer can take about 44 minutes. NASA's Mars planning paper says crews will need tools that help them watch their own health and decide without waiting for the ground. Astra Vigil is one small piece of that need: a watcher that sits on board and answers at once.

 

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"«Умные» футболки в космосе: как отслеживают жизненно важные показатели космонавтов | Пикабу" ]

HOW IT WORKS

1. Sensors send data to the main computer. The plan uses a chest strap (Polar H10) and cabin sensors.

2. Each day the computer turns the raw numbers into one row of six values: heart rate, HRV, SpO2, sleep, core temperature and exercise.

3. It builds the person's own baseline from their last 30 days. It needs at least 14 days before it judges. Days that were already an alert are left out, so a slow slide is not learned as normal.

4. It finds a z-score. This counts how many standard deviations today is from the person's own average. The sign is set so that "worse" is always clear.

5. Two simple rules decide. Rule S: one signal is 2.0 SD or more worse for 2 days in a row. Rule M: two or more signals are 2.5 SD or more worse within 2 days.

6. The status is learning, normal, watch or alert. An alert is held for 3 days so it does not flicker.

7. The console writes the reason in plain words from a template, shows the rule and the numbers, and lists saved NASA records that match the signal. A "guard" blocks words that sound like a diagnosis.

Example: an HRV baseline has a mean of 60 and an SD of 5. Day 1 HRV is 48 (z = -2.4), so the status is watch. Day 2 HRV is 47 (z = -2.6), so Rule S raises an alert.

 

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- It works on board, so there is no wait for the ground.

- It compares each person with their own normal, not with a crowd.

- No AI model makes decisions. The detector is plain Python and NumPy. The same input always gives the same output, and every alert shows the rule and the numbers behind it.

- Privacy tiers protect trust in a small crew. Tier 0: the crew member sees their own data. Tier 1: the medical role sees only the trend direction, and only with consent. Tier 2: a short status word can leave for Earth. Messages wait in a store-and-forward outbox and go out with the light-time delay.

- Every access is written to an audit log linked with SHA-256, so any change is easy to spot.

The goal is to give future Moon and Mars crews an early, private, explainable signal, so people can look at sleep, workload and rest and talk to their medical officer early.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Artemis II Success Opens Door for Peru's Spaceport Dreams While Revealing Critical Astronaut Health Challenges | Planet News" ]

 

WORKS OFFLINE

The detector, the saved NASA records (22 records fetched on 2026-10-20), the explanations, the console, the privacy views and the audit log all run on the device. A headless-browser test of the console saw requests to localhost only. Only refreshing the NASA records needs a network, and that step is optional.

 

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"ESA - Astro Pi units running students' experiments on the ISS" ]

RESULTS (SIMULATED DATA ONLY)

We made 4 fictional astronauts (Kestrel, Lyra, Mira and Vega), 600 days each, with planted events. At the default setting (400 runs) the detector caught 99.8% of planted 2-day HRV drops and 98.0% of planted 3-day changes in HRV, heart rate and sleep. But it also raised about 24 false alerts per 1,000 crew-days, which is about 14 per person over 600 days. With stricter thresholds (2.5 / 3.0 SD, 150 runs) false alerts fell to 3.2 per 1,000 crew-days (about 1.9 per person), and it still caught 96.0% and 96.7%. We have not chosen the final setting, because it must come from real data. There is no honest single accuracy number for real astronauts.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Generated image 1" ]

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

Python 3.10+, FastAPI, Uvicorn, NumPy, SQLite, WebSocket, and a console made with plain JavaScript and HTML canvas (no framework, no CDN). An optional local language model (Ollama) may only reword explanations, behind the guard. Tests use pytest and httpx (33 tests for the console). Our showcase website uses the same detector, Three.js r160, three bundled open fonts, matching English and Bangla text, and 850 passing test cases. Planned test-bench hardware: Raspberry Pi 5 or Jetson Orin Nano, Polar H10 chest strap, ESP32 with SCD40 and BME280 sensors, and an offline router with Mosquitto (MQTT). The code license is Apache-2.0.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Raspberry Pi 5, 4GB RAM - buy at BerryBase" ]

 

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"NVIDIA® Jetson Orin™ Nano Super Developer Kit AI edge computer – IOT Store" ]

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Programma esp32 stm32 arduino microcontroller firmware embedded iot apparaat ontwikkelen" ]

WHAT IS CREATIVE

A watcher that learns each person's own normal; privacy tiers made for small crews far from home; plain-math alerts with a built-in explanation; honest reporting of false alarms and weak spots; and a full English and Bangla interface.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Nicolas Beaufils – Product Designer" ]

 

LIMITS AND NEXT STEPS

All numbers come from simulated data. The sensor bridge and the daily summary maker are not built yet. Nothing has been tested on flight hardware. Slow drifts are a known weak spot. The live NASA refresh was tested only with mock responses. Next: build the sensor bridge, test the detector on a public ground study (bed rest or isolation), tune thresholds, test on a Raspberry Pi 5, and ask a flight surgeon or space-medicine team to review the alert words and the privacy tiers.
